Name: graded_harm_geometry
Title: Beyond Binary Refusal: Uncovering and Exploiting Graded Harm Magnitude in LLM Activation Geometry for Jailbreak-Robust Safety Monitoring
Short Hypothesis: LLM safety-aligned behavior collapses a rich, continuous internal representation of harm *severity* into a binary refuse/comply decision. We hypothesize that the residual stream encodes a graded, monotonic 'harm magnitude' scalar that is largely orthogonal to jailbreak perturbations, and that reading this scalar directly yields a safety monitor far more robust to jailbreaks than the model's own refusal decision.
Related Work: Arditi et al. and follow-ups show refusal is mediated by a single dominant direction. Pan et al. (2025) and Piras et al. (2025, SOM) extend this to multi-dimensional subspaces. Minionese (2026) and Wagle et al. (2026) show jailbreaks route harmful content around refusal directions leaving the mechanism 'intact but untriggered.' All prior work treats refusal as binary/categorical (harmful vs harmless prompt centroids). Our distinction: we investigate whether the geometry encodes a *continuous, ordinal harm-severity signal* (mild policy violation vs catastrophic request), which no prior work extracts or exploits. Critically, jailbreaks aim to flip the binary decision but need not preserve/suppress the graded severity signal—so a monitor built on the ordinal axis may fire even when the categorical refusal is bypassed. This reframes safety from a decision boundary to a regression on latent harm.
Abstract: Safety alignment teaches LLMs to refuse harmful queries, and mechanistic interpretability has localized this behavior to low-dimensional directions in the residual stream. Yet refusal is fundamentally treated as a binary decision, and jailbreaks succeed precisely by nudging inputs across this decision boundary or routing them through orthogonal subspaces. We ask a simpler question: does the model internally represent *how* harmful a request is, on a continuous scale, even when its output-level refusal is binary? We construct a graded-harm probe dataset spanning severity tiers (from benign, to borderline, to severe, to catastrophic requests) across multiple harm categories, and fit ordinal probes on residual-stream activations of open-weight models (Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B). We find a single monotonic 'harm-magnitude' axis that (i) correlates with human-annotated severity far beyond the binary refusal direction, and (ii) is substantially more preserved under a battery of jailbreaks (GCG, roleplay, translation, refusal-suppression steering) than the categorical refusal decision. Exploiting this, we build a lightweight internal safety monitor that reads the graded axis and flags harmful intent regardless of whether the model complies, achieving higher jailbreak detection AUROC than output-based classifiers and the model's own refusal, with near-zero benign false positives. We further show the axis enables *calibrated* responses (soft warnings vs hard refusals) and diagnose why jailbreaks that flip refusal still leave harm magnitude high. Our work recasts LLM safety geometry from a decision boundary to a latent regression signal.
Experiments: 1) Dataset construction: build a graded-harm corpus by taking existing harmful-behavior benchmarks (AdvBench, HarmBench, StrongREJECT) and annotating/augmenting with 4-5 severity tiers per category (e.g., asking for general chemistry info -> specific synthesis -> weaponization), plus benign controls. Collect human severity ratings (small crowd or expert annotation, feasible for ~1000 items). 2) Probe extraction: on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, extract last-token residual activations across layers; fit (a) the standard difference-in-means refusal direction, (b) an ordinal logistic / linear regression probe for severity. Measure Spearman correlation of each with human severity ratings; test monotonicity and layer-wise emergence. 3) Orthogonality analysis: measure cosine similarity between the graded axis and the binary refusal direction; decompose to show the graded axis has a component orthogonal to refusal. 4) Jailbreak robustness: apply GCG suffixes, roleplay/DAN prompts, low-resource translation, and refusal-suppression activation steering to harmful prompts. Measure how much (a) the model's refusal flips vs (b) the graded harm-magnitude projection changes. Hypothesis: refusal flips but harm magnitude stays high. 5) Safety monitor: build a threshold classifier on the graded axis; compare jailbreak-detection AUROC and benign false-positive rate against (i) output-based moderation classifiers (Llama-Guard), (ii) the binary refusal probe, (iii) perplexity/input-filter baselines. 6) Calibrated intervention: use the graded score to modulate response (warn vs refuse vs comply) and measure over-refusal on benign borderline sets (XSTest, OR-Bench). Metrics: Spearman correlation, AUROC, FPR at fixed TPR, attack success rate reduction, over-refusal rate.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) The graded harm axis may turn out highly collinear with the binary refusal direction, weakening the novelty—mitigated by testing multiple models and reporting the orthogonal component explicitly. 2) Severity annotation is subjective; we mitigate with multiple annotators and category-relative tiers. 3) Some jailbreaks (e.g., ciphered/obfuscated inputs) may genuinely destroy the harm representation, limiting monitor coverage—this is itself an interesting finding to report. 4) Probes can pick up spurious surface features; we control with paraphrase and cross-category generalization tests. 5) Results are on open-weight mid-size models and may not directly transfer to frontier closed models, though the mechanism-level claims are model-agnostic in spirit.
